The Summer of the Storm is an original Tafiya Estate story. It shows a community meeting a real danger calmly and sensibly, with the children helping in safe and useful ways while the adults handle the risk. It celebrates quick eyes, cool heads, and the simple truth that hard things become possible when neighbours face them together.

All day the heat had pressed down like a heavy blanket, and not a single leaf had stirred. Then, late in the afternoon, the sky over the estate turned a strange, bruised green, and the air went suddenly still. Boma looked up from the veranda and felt the first cool breath of wind. "A big storm's coming," he said. "A really big one."

image.note: Boma on a veranda looking up at an ominous green-tinged sky over modern estate rooftops; palm fronds just beginning to stir; heavy, waiting stillness

pages.text: His mum was already moving, calling the little ones inside and unplugging the television. "Help me shut the windows," she said. Boma ran from room to room, latching every one. Outside, the wind was rising fast now, snatching at the washing on the line and sending a plastic chair skittering across the yard.

image.note: Boma latching a window from inside as the wind whips a washing line outside; his mum ushering small children in; a plastic chair tumbling across the yard beyond the glass

pages.text: The storm broke with a crack of thunder that rattled the panes. Rain came down not in drops but in sheets, so thick that Boma could barely see the gate from the window. Lightning lit the whole estate white for an instant, then plunged it back into grey. The power flickered once, twice, and went out with a soft click.

image.note: View through a rain-streaked window: sheets of rain blurring the estate, a fork of lightning; inside dim as the lights cut out; Boma's face lit by the flash

pages.text: Boma's little sister clutched his arm at the thunder. "It's alright," he said, fetching the lamp and switching it on. "It's only noise. The house is strong." They sat together in the warm circle of lamplight, listening to the rain drum on the roof, while his mum lit candles in the other rooms. The storm roared on outside.

image.note: A cosy lamp-lit room amid the storm; Boma with an arm round his small sister, both calm; his mum placing a candle nearby; rain streaming down the dark window

pages.text: After an hour the rain had not eased, and Boma noticed something worrying at the window. The yard was no longer just wet. It was filling up. A wide brown pool had spread across it, creeping steadily towards the veranda step, higher every time he looked. "Mum," he called. "The water isn't draining away."

image.note: Boma at the window pointing down at a spreading brown pool covering the yard, water near the veranda step; his mum coming over with the lamp, concerned; rain still falling hard

pages.text: His mum peered out and frowned. "The gutter must be blocked," she said. "If the water can't run off, it'll come right up to the door." Through the downpour Boma could see other neighbours at their windows too, all watching the same brown water rise across the estate. Something had to be done, and soon.

image.note: Multiple lit windows across the dark, flooded estate, worried faces at each; the brown water rising between the houses; rain slanting through lamplight

pages.text: When the rain finally softened to a steady patter, the neighbours came out onto their verandas, calling to one another across the water. Boma pulled on his rain boots and waded carefully to where his dad and Remigius stood by the main drain. And there Boma spotted it: a great tangle of leaves and a lodged plastic sheet, choking the grate completely.

image.note: Adults in rain gear gathered at a flooded main drain in fading rain; Boma in boots pointing at a grate clogged with a thick mat of leaves and a stuck plastic sheet; brown water pooled around them

pages.text: "That's it," said his dad. "That's why the water's got nowhere to go." But the grate was heavy and the rubbish packed tight. Remigius shook his head. "This is too much for two pairs of hands," he said. Boma looked around at all the lit verandas. "Then let's get more hands," he said.

image.note: Boma's dad and Remigius crouched at the stubborn clogged grate, straining; Boma standing back, glancing round at the many lit verandas with an idea; rain easing

pages.text: Boma went door to door with his dad, and one by one the neighbours came. Some brought rakes, some brought buckets, and old Baba Sule brought a bright torch to light the work. Nobody let the children near the deep, fast water. Instead the young ones formed a line further back, passing armfuls of cleared leaves to the bins.

image.note: A line of neighbours working together at the drain by torchlight: adults at the grate, children safely further back passing bundles of leaves to bins; buckets and rakes; teamwork in the wet dusk

pages.text: Together the adults heaved the heavy grate aside and dragged out the sodden, tangled mass. For a long moment nothing happened. Then, with a deep, gurgling rush, the trapped water began to spin and pour away down the open drain. A great cheer went up from every veranda around the flooded yard.

image.note: The freed drain gulping down a swirling rush of brown water; adults stepping back triumphant; neighbours on verandas cheering, arms raised; torchlight and relief

pages.text: By the time the last of the water had drained, it was very late and everyone was soaked through. But no one went straight to bed. The neighbours gathered under the estate hut, where someone had a flask of hot tea, and they laughed and talked about the storm they had beaten together. Boma had never felt so proud of his home.

image.note: Neighbours sheltering together under the thatched estate hut at night, sharing tea from a flask, laughing wearily; lamplight; Boma among them, tired and proud; dripping raincoats

pages.text: "You spotted that drain, young man," said Baba Sule, resting a hand on Boma's shoulder. "Quick eyes." Boma smiled but shook his head. "Everyone dug it out, not just me," he said. And that, he thought, was the real point. One person had noticed, but it had taken the whole estate to put it right.

image.note: Baba Sule's hand on Boma's shoulder under the hut, both smiling; the tired, happy group of neighbours around them; warm lamplight against the night

pages.text: Boma woke the next morning to a world washed clean. The sky was a soft, gentle blue, the puddles shrank in the warm sun, and the air smelled fresh and green. Birds were already busy in the dripping trees. The yard that had been a brown lake the night before was just a yard again, shining wet.

image.note: A bright fresh morning after the storm: clear blue sky, shrinking puddles, dripping green trees, birds about; the ordinary yard glistening in gentle sun

pages.text: On his way to school Boma passed the drain, running clear and free. Neighbours he barely knew before now waved and called his name. The storm had been frightening, but it had left something good behind. His estate, Boma decided, was the kind of place that pulled together when it mattered most.

image.note: Boma walking to school past the clear, free-flowing drain, waving to friendly neighbours; sunny, restored estate; a settled, happy mood
